deck.title: SentiLab
deck.talk: Five-minute slot: talk, then a live demo

notes.text: AI agents can now propose chiplet layouts in minutes, and a thermal simulator judges every one. We ran one published layout through two releases of the same open simulator, with byte-identical input files. Version 6.0 says 119 degrees; 7.0 says 241. That's 2.6 times the temperature rise. SentiLab is built so agents propose, challenge each other and keep the evidence. All of it is simulated, not silicon.

content.title: Same chips, same power, same input files: 119 or 241 degrees?

figure.alt: Heat maps of the CPU-DRAM layout's chip layer in HotSpot 6.0 and 7.0 on one colour scale, from byte-identical input files: chip-layer grid maxima of 119 and 241 degrees, 2.6 times the temperature rise. The frozen gate statistic reads 115.93 and 232.67 degrees.

content.line: SentiLab: agents propose, challenge each other and keep the evidence behind every result.
content.caption: The CPU-DRAM layout's chip layer on a 64 by 64 grid; the ring marks the hottest cell. 119 and 241 are chip-layer grid maxima (119.07 C and 240.53 C). The frozen gate statistic, the maximum native block output under centre mapping, is 115.93 C and 232.67 C; in 7.0 that maximum is a substrate block, not a chip. Run 23:41 to 23:44 UTC. Simulated, not silicon.

notes.text: Here's where it opens. Follow the hottest cell down through the modeled layers: between the spreader and the sink, the difference is 4 kelvin in 6.0 and 142 in 7.0. The public source computes that link differently. An outside team ran both versions with the detailed 3-D mode off and got the same answer, as reported by them.

content.title: The difference opens between two modeled layers.

figure.alt: Exploded view of the modeled layers of the CPU-DRAM layout, at the same x/y grid index under each run's hottest chip-layer cell. HotSpot 6.0 goes 119, 116, 106, 102 degrees; 7.0 goes 241, 235, 228, 86: a 4.04 K against a 141.77 K difference between the spreader and sink nodes. A separate panel gives the difference of independently located layer maxima, spreader minus sink: 3.25 K in 6.0, about 4.20 K in two finite-element codes and 141.84 K in 7.0.

content.text: In public source, the spreader-to-sink link is `rz(n)` in HotSpot 6.0 and `rz(n)/2 + rz(n+1)/2` in 7.0, and the sink's `rz` includes convection. Our old results used 7.0.
content.credit: An outside team ran both versions with the detailed 3-D mode off: both give 75.37 C and 115.29 C, as reported by them.
content.caption: The CPU-DRAM layout: each run's hottest chip-layer cell, then the same x/y grid index through the modeled layers, shown exploded. Spreader to sink: 4.04 K in 6.0, 141.77 K in 7.0. Modeled nodes, not a copper layer. This localizes the difference; it does not by itself show a single cause. Panel at right: Difference of independently located layer maxima; FE nodal versus HotSpot grid readouts. One configured model, simulated.

notes.text: A person asked one question at 12:43. Thirty-two minutes later an agent reading the source named a suspect, and a second confirmed it. A third, run by another person, modeled it from public code. Then one agent proposed stopping our own public run, two agreed, and it halted under five minutes later. We withdrew those temperatures in public.

content.title: The day in detail: 31 October into 1 November 2026, UTC, from the room record.
content.note: Each line matches at least one room record (room, message, author, time), listed in the repository's TIMELINE-VERIFY.md.

rows.text: A person asks why the study was inconclusive and how to match the published reference design, and asks three agents to research separately, then challenge each other.
Three agents seal their findings before reading each other's (13:08 to 13:15; one had seen a one-line preview), then attack each other's reports (13:18).
One agent's sealed findings suspect that the simulator puts part of the heat-sink convection term between the spreader and the sink. Marked as a hypothesis.
A second agent's source reviewer confirms that the link includes half of the sink's resistance, which carries convection.

A third agent, run by another person under a separate account, posts a simplified model built from public source. It had read the hypothesis: an informed peer, not a blind check. The older link form lands within 0.4 K of the paper on both original layouts; the newer form raises the rise about 2.6 times.
Two other agents rerun that model; every row reproduces (14:38 and 14:45).

Saved simulator output, no new solve: a 51.10 to 52.40 K difference between matching spreader and heat-sink nodes, across eight retained probes (four floorplans at two grid sizes). A separate parser confirms two of them at 14:53.
The peer model's version 2 fixes both review findings on version 1: it uses the simulator's own centre rule and refuses to return a result that has not converged.
In the simplified model the error stretches gaps between layouts 2.3 to 3.7 times and reorders 8 to 9% of pairs, so old comparisons between our own layouts cannot stand either.
An agent flags that the public loop still runs on that engine and proposes a notice plus no new runs. A second agent agrees at 15:52, a third at 15:54.
The stop is written at 15:56:59 and read back: the running job settles, and its ledger, chain and charges are kept. Another agent's public readback confirms it at 16:02.
The notice withdrawing those temperatures is merged, deployed and checked in a real browser.
Four production reads by another agent match the reviewed source.
Our public test case for the paper's two layouts goes up, with our own numbers withheld so outside checks stay independent.
An outside team runs both simulator versions on that case, 39 minutes later: 75.48 C and 115.94 C in 6.0, 123.42 C and 232.67 C in 7.0, as reported by them.

The fixed test runs from 23:41 to 23:44, and the operator reports PASS: 75.48 C and 115.93 C against the paper's 75.48 C and 115.94 C. A second reviewer re-derives it independently by 00:05 on 1 November.
A second outside team reports its own finite-element result, 1 h 41 after the case went up: 78.060 C and 122.252 C, as reported by them.

content.title: Gate zero: what runs, what passes, and the wording fixed before the result.
rules: The older simulator version (6.0), at the paper's conditions: 45 mm interposer, 64 by 64 grid, 45 C ambient, the paper's block-centre metric.
Each published layout gets one run plus a replay in a fresh process. Both must land within 1.0 K, and the replay's output must be byte-identical.
Verdicts, most definitive first: FAIL, ERROR, INCOMPLETE, PASS. Anything missing or unsettled is INCOMPLETE, never PASS.
Two more published points (75.47 C and 94.89 C) are deferred: no runs here, and they cannot pass or fail this gate.
content.source: Ma et al., TAP-2.5D, DATE 2021: Fig. 6(a) at 75.48 C and Fig. 5(a) at 115.94 C.
content.wordingTitle: Wording fixed before the result, for all three outcomes

result.label: PASS
result.verification: Verified by the operator and independently re-derived from signed raw outputs by a second reviewer.
detail: Run: 12 calls under a grant opened 23:41 UTC, from the merged build, one at a time, finished by 23:44. Each call was reserved, admitted, launched, receipted, settled and tagged.
Re-derived at 00:05 UTC from the saved artifacts by a second reviewer: 37 signatures, the 25-entry chain, every cell of all 12 grids. No solver was run for it.
Replays byte-identical. At a 32 by 32 grid: 75.46 C and 115.28 C. Kept apart from the gate statistic: chiplet-centre means 75.475 C and 115.935 C, active-grid peaks 75.48 C and 119.07 C.
At each run's hottest cell, spreader-to-sink difference: 1.24 K (6.0) against 55.31 K (7.0) on layout A, 4.04 K against 141.77 K on layout B.
Compute, for the validation container only: 23.0 CPU-seconds of 562 reserved (cap 600); the solver used 17.86. Not the cost of the build, the models or the project.
result.comparator: Version comparison on the same layouts and readout: version 7.0 gives 123.42 C and 232.67 C, 48 to 117 K above the paper.

content.title: The outside-team receipts, exactly, and what we do not count as evidence.

facts.label: Case
facts.text: Our public parameter sheet for the paper's two layouts (commit af66bcfc), posted at 22:22 UTC with our own numbers withheld.

facts.label: Reproduction
facts.text: An outside team: both simulator versions built from source and run on that case: 75.48 C and 115.94 C in 6.0, 123.42 C and 232.67 C in 7.0; with the detailed 3-D mode off, both give 75.37 C and 115.29 C. As reported by them.

facts.label: Finite element
facts.text: A second outside team (public repository, frozen report at commit c73d642b): second-order elements on the finest mesh, about 1.6 to 1.7 million unknowns: 78.060 C and 122.252 C, +2.58 K and +6.31 K over the paper. As reported by them.

facts.label: Exposure
facts.text: The finite-element run is a separate implementation: its author declares no reading of peer values before freezing at 23:45 UTC. Our team's values were posted in the shared help room from 23:04 UTC, and to that team directly at 23:18, which shows they were available, not that they were read. The paper's targets were known.

facts.label: Checked
facts.text: A second reviewer verified the finite-element team's 48-file manifest and frozen hashes, and recomputed the values from saved results. Their mesh and field files are omitted, so this is a check of saved values.

facts.label: Limit
facts.text: A configured-model comparison, not silicon validation, with no certified 0.1 K error bound. Earlier the same team ran our closed-form slab test (commit 32f3ed1a).
